items.q: Which of these is a non-financial reason for setting up in business?
opts: Receiving dividends
Building up wealth to sell the business later
Earning a higher income
Being your own boss
items.why: Independence and control over your work are non-financial reasons. The others are all about money.

items.q: In SMART objectives, as used in the AQA specification, what does the A stand for?
opts: Accountable
Achievable
Agreed
Ambitious
items.why: The AQA specification uses Accountable: someone is responsible for meeting the objective. Many textbooks say Achievable, so be careful.

items.q: What is opportunity cost?
opts: The cost of starting a business
The money lost when a decision goes wrong
The next best alternative given up when a choice is made
The total cost of all the options available
items.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up. If a business spends £50,000 on a new machine, the opportunity cost might be the marketing campaign it could have run instead.

items.q: Which of these is one of the characteristics of entrepreneurs listed in the specification?
opts: Risk averse
Resilient
Cautious
Specialised
items.why: The specification lists risk taker, resilient, focused, passionate, innovative and adaptable.

items.q: What is the main purpose of a business plan?
opts: To guarantee that a business will succeed
To set out the business's aims, strategy and financial forecasts, which can help it plan and raise finance
To set the prices of the products
To meet a legal requirement for all businesses
items.why: A business plan helps the owner think things through and shows lenders and investors that the idea has been planned. It does not guarantee success.

items.q: What does competitiveness mean?
opts: How aggressive a business's adverts are
The number of competitors in a market
The ability of a business or product to outperform its rivals
Selling at the lowest price
items.why: Competitiveness is about outperforming rivals, for example through price, quality, brand or service.

items.q: What does unlimited liability mean?
opts: The owner can only lose the money they invested
The business does not have to pay tax
The owner is personally responsible for all of the business's debts
The business can borrow as much as it likes
items.why: With unlimited liability, a sole trader's personal possessions, such as their house, can be used to pay the business's debts.

items.q: Which form of business can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange?
opts: Sole trader
Private limited company (Ltd)
Public limited company (plc)
Worker co-operative
items.why: Only a plc can offer its shares to the general public. A Ltd can only sell shares privately, for example to family and friends.

items.q: Who owns a worker co-operative?
opts: Shareholders on the stock exchange
The government
The people who work in it
The customers
items.why: A worker co-operative is owned and run by its employees. A consumer co-operative is owned by its customers and a producer co-operative by its producers.

items.q: Which best describes a social enterprise?
opts: A business with social or environmental aims that reinvests most of its profit into those aims
A business owned by the government
Any business that uses social media
A charity that does not trade
items.why: Social enterprises trade like other businesses, but their main purpose is social or environmental.

items.q: Which of these is an external stakeholder?
opts: Shareholders
Suppliers
Employees
Managers
items.why: External stakeholders are outside the business: customers, suppliers, other creditors, the community and the government.

items.q: What does dividend yield measure?
opts: The total profit paid out to shareholders
The change in share price over a year
The number of shares in issue
The annual dividend per share as a percentage of the share price
items.why: Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ share price × 100. It shows the return from dividends for each £1 invested at today's price.

items.q: Which of these is most likely to cause a company's share price to fall?
opts: The company announces a large new contract
The company warns that profit will be lower than expected
The company's main rival goes out of business
Interest rates on savings accounts fall
items.why: Share prices reflect what investors expect about future profit. A profit warning lowers those expectations, so demand for the shares falls.

items.q: A plc's share price rises by 20% on the stock exchange. What happens to the money the company has?
opts: Nothing directly. The shares are traded between investors, so the company does not receive the extra money
The company's profit rises by 20%
The company must pay a higher dividend
The company receives 20% more cash
items.why: Shares traded on the stock exchange change hands between investors. A higher share price helps the company if it issues new shares later, but it does not receive cash from the rise itself.

items.q: What is primary market research?
opts: Research collected first-hand for a specific purpose
Research that has already been published by others
The first research a business ever does
Research carried out by the government
items.why: Primary research, such as surveys, interviews and test marketing, is collected by or for the business for its own purpose.

items.q: What is qualitative data?
opts: Data in the form of numbers and percentages
Data that has been checked for accuracy
Information about opinions, feelings and reasons, which is not usually numerical
Data from secondary sources only
items.why: Qualitative data tells you why people think or act as they do. Quantitative data is numerical.

items.q: A survey result has a 95% confidence level. What does this mean?
opts: 95% of the people asked agreed
The business can be 95% confident that the true figure for the whole population lies within the confidence interval
The result is 95% accurate
The survey asked 95% of customers
items.why: The confidence level tells you how sure you can be that the true value lies inside the confidence interval.

items.q: What does a wider confidence interval tell you about a survey result?
opts: The confidence level is higher
The result is less precise
The result is more accurate
More people agreed
items.why: A wide interval means the true figure could be anywhere in a big range. Bigger samples usually give narrower intervals.

items.q: What is market mapping used for?
opts: Planning delivery routes
Showing where products sit compared with rivals on two features, to spot gaps in the market
Working out a business's market share
Finding the location of a business's customers
items.why: A market map plots brands on two axes, such as price and quality, to show how they are positioned and where there may be a gap.

items.q: Which of these would most reduce the reliability of a survey?
opts: Using a large random sample
Asking clear questions
A small sample that does not represent the target market
Checking the results against secondary data
items.why: If the sample is small or not representative, the results may not reflect what the whole target market thinks.
